To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

low-dose computed tomography screening for lung cancer was associated with a higher rate of false-positive results than the National Lung Screening Trial, and the rate of adherence to screening was low.
the rate of positive screening test was higher in the community setting compared with the NLST and that invasive diagnostic follow-up was low and uncomplicated.
community-based LDCT screening for lung cancer was associated with a high false positive rate, a low adherence to screening, and a high proportion of late follow-up.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development, evaluation, and implementation of new technologies in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer.
how the NLST results can best be translated into clinical practice and public policy.
the development, implementation, and evaluation of community-based interventions for the promotion of health and the prevention of disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
community-based screening is not ready for prime time.
CT screening in the community setting has not been proven to reduce lung cancer mortality and should be performed in an integrated setting.

community-based LDCT lung screening has the potential to achieve results similar to that of the NLST, but only when the screening is performed in a highly integrated and structured setting, with close coordination of the screening, diagnostic, and treatment components of the program.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
community-based LDCT lung cancer screening programs are feasible and can be implemented, but the results are less favorable than in a highly structured program.
community low-dose CT screening is feasible but not ideal.
the NLST results are not easily generalizable to community settings.
The main takeaway from our work is that

community screening is a complex process that requires careful attention to the details of the screening program, as well as a high level of engagement with the primary care providers and participants.
the NLST is not the only way to reduce lung cancer mortality.
the community setting, as currently practiced, is not an appropriate setting to deploy LDCT lung cancer screening.
